name: Frankincense and moringa wrinkle remedy

lead: This is a skin-care recipe preserved at the end of the Edwin Smith Surgical Papyrus, an ancient Egyptian text. It describes an ointment meant to remove wrinkles and make an old man look young, and is commonly summarised as frankincense gum, moringa (ben) oil and wax, sometimes with other plant ingredients.

It has circulated in modern anti-aging writing as a historical example of an emollient wrinkle treatment. Frankincense and plant oils are used in current skin-care products as moisturising and soothing ingredients, so people interested in natural anti-aging sometimes try home versions.

paras: Modern adaptations are generally blends of a frankincense-containing product with a carrier oil such as moringa oil, used as a night-time facial oil or balm. There is no standard formula, because translations of the original disagree on some ingredients.

Essential oils and resins can cause contact allergy or irritation in some people, and a patch test is the usual dermatological precaution. The original text is a historical recipe, not a studied treatment.

lead: The "Egyptian anti-wrinkle" recipe is an ointment preserved at the end of the Edwin Smith Surgical Papyrus, published in 1930 by James Henry Breasted. A Wellcome Collection facsimile of the papyrus section describes it as a recipe for an ointment for removing wrinkles that would make an old man look young.[1]

Secondary accounts summarise its contents as gum of frankincense, a plant oil identified as moringa or balanites, and wax, ground with other plant material into a viscous paste; translations differ on some ingredients, and one ingredient name defied identification in Breasted's time. It is used in modern natural-skin-care circles as an example of a historical anti-wrinkle treatment.
infobox: Ancient Egypt; Edwin Smith Surgical Papyrus [1]

paras: The recipe sits at the back of the papyrus, which is otherwise known as a surgical text; it is a short cosmetic recipe sometimes titled as transforming an old man into a youth.[1] The Wellcome Collection holds a 1962 reproduction of the photograph of that section from Breasted's edition.[1]

Accounts of its ingredients vary. Some describe frankincense gum, moringa oil and wax; others list balanites oil and rush-nut or cyperus, ground together, with some mentioning a fermented juice. Milk, often attached to the recipe in popular retellings, is not part of the wrinkle recipes in those accounts but appears in other Egyptian skin preparations.[2]

Frankincense (Boswellia resin) and moringa oil are available as cosmetic ingredients, and blogs and brands cite the papyrus as heritage for anti-wrinkle products. Proponents describe the oils as nourishing and the resin as skin-firming.
No studies found. No clinical trial has tested the reconstructed ancient recipe on wrinkles.
